findings.title: Rivalry is more than a yes/no label
findings.finding: A study of 7,670 games from 2008–2018 found that favorites covered less often in some rivalry settings, especially games between two non-Power Five teams. Most closing spreads still incorporated rivalry dynamics. These are spread results, not an automatic increase in outright upset probability.
findings.test: Track each side’s rivalry intensity, recent series, venue, current coaching era and conference era. Test an effect on both expected margin and result variability. Do not apply a blanket rivalry bonus.
findings.sourceLabel: Cox, Journal of Economics and Finance (2026)

findings.title: Rivalry can change risk-taking
findings.finding: NFL play-by-play research and a laboratory experiment found more risk-taking in rivalry settings. That supports examining fourth-down decisions and aggressive play, but does not establish that college underdogs always benefit.
findings.test: Measure fourth-down attempts relative to field position and score, plus explosive-play and turnover volatility. Motivation could help a favorite dominate or leave an underdog exposed.
findings.sourceLabel: To et al., Academy of Management Journal (2018)

findings.title: Travel: distance and body-clock time are different
findings.finding: A 2025 college-football study of 6,245 games found no clear effect of time-zone changes and kickoff time on performance relative to the spread. It excluded noncontinental locations, so it cannot settle Hawaii or overseas travel questions.
findings.test: Record origin-to-venue distance, time-zone change, kickoff in the visitor’s home zone, rest days and repeated road trips. Arrival timing must remain unknown unless sourced. Distance is not itself proof of fatigue.
findings.sourceLabel: Tenan, Rezai & Vigotsky, American Journal of Epidemiology (2025)

findings.title: Stadium effects can hit offense and defense differently
findings.finding: A 12-season college-football study associated travel distance with higher home-team scoring and crowd size/density with lower visiting-team scoring. This supports separating offensive and defensive effects rather than assuming one stadium penalty.
findings.test: Combine opponent-adjusted home/road offense and defense with crowd, venue familiarity, local kickoff and weather. Our first simple home/road revision failed the later-game test; a published association does not validate our implementation.
findings.sourceLabel: McMahon et al., Southern Economic Journal (2024)

findings.title: Coaching records need context
findings.finding: A college-football coaching-change study found little benefit for the poorest-performing teams and worse subsequent results for some middling programs, compared with matched teams retaining their coach. A new coach is not an automatic boost.
findings.test: Separate coach-versus-school from coach-versus-coach records. Record head coach, coordinators, play-caller, tenure and roster continuity. Compare actual margins with what team strength predicted; a 5–0 record as a heavy favorite may add little information.
findings.sourceLabel: Adler, Berry & Doherty, Social Science Quarterly (2013)

findings.title: Motivation and revenge must be observable before kickoff
findings.finding: College-football momentum research found no systematic relationship between several momentum measures and game outcomes after accounting for differences between teams. A previous big win or loss alone does not establish a letdown or rebound.
findings.test: Distinguish prior upset wins, close losses, humiliating rematch losses, rest and upcoming opponents. Source former-team connections, trophy games and direct coach/player statements. Do not infer that an entire roster wants it more.

findings.title: First road start is a testable combination
findings.finding: The NCAA introduced optional FBS coach-to-player helmet communication in 2024, with communication ending at 15 seconds on the play clock or the snap. That is one reason older crowd-and-QB patterns may not transfer unchanged to today’s game.
findings.test: Verify the starter, career starts, road starts, snaps with this center and replacement experience. Test inexperienced QB × new center × hostile venue × opponent pass rush. These interacting conditions are hypotheses until tested on later games.

coverage: Selective sourced injury watch covering three teams, not a comprehensive or automatically refreshed injury feed. Team-unit play indicators are loaded separately. Individual pressure rates, interior versus edge pressure, five-player OL continuity, verified replacement starts and snap counts are not systematically connected. Existing absences may already be reflected in recent results; adding a new penalty could double-count them. No numeric injury adjustment is applied.
priorities: Verify starting center, tackles, interior DL and edge availability with report date and applicable game.
Measure protection and rushing matchups separately; sacks are not the same thing as pressures, and team rates are not individual line grades.
Build dated coach/coordinator tenures and directional rivalry labels; retain provenance and avoid using newer surveys as if known in old seasons.
Add venue coordinates/time zones and actual kickoff times; do not fabricate travel itineraries or arrival dates.
Evaluate a small predeclared set of interactions on multiple seasons, then new games; compare winner accuracy, margin error and probability reliability with matched-time market data.
